== Current conclusion ==

The Glasgow name developed from the Scottish place-name Glasgow and was used as a personal locative—''de Glasgu'', ''de Glascu'', ''de Glasgw'' and related forms—before it became a stable hereditary surname. The surviving records do not prove that every medieval bearer belonged to one family or that the surname began with a single founder.

The earliest bearer so far identified in this study is [[Space:Roger of Glasgow|Roger de Glasgu]], who witnessed an episcopal act between about 1175 and 1199.<ref name="Roger">''Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis'', vol. I (Edinburgh, 1843), no. 90, p. 77; [https://archive.org/details/registrumepiscv175glasuoft Internet Archive].</ref> Dublin guild records then show Richard, Robert, Gilbert and Alexander son of Robert in the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. These records demonstrate repeated personal use, but not one pedigree.

== John de Glasgu and Bishop Gamelin ==

On 2 February 1259, an act named [[Space:John de Glasgu|John de Glasgu]] as chaplain of Bishop Gamelin of St Andrews.<ref name="JohnGamelin">''Registrum Prioratus Sancti Andree'' (Bannatyne Club, Edinburgh, 1841), p. 173; [https://archive.org/details/libercartarump6900edinuoft Internet Archive]. See also People of Medieval Scotland, person no. 3404; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/3404/ PoMS].</ref> The record does not call John “Master”, identify his parents or make him Gamelin's brother. Gamelin's political and family connections therefore cannot be used as John's ancestry.

A broad-dated Dunipace witness with the same name is probably the chaplain because Richard de Stickley appeared in both witness groups. The identification is not certain because the Dunipace act does not repeat John's office.<ref name="CambusJohn">''Registrum Monasterii S. Marie de Cambuskenneth'', no. 81; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/07280081 DEEDS 07280081]; People of Medieval Scotland, source no. 5639; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/source/5639/ PoMS].</ref>

== From locative to surname ==

The records support a gradual transition:

* twelfth- and thirteenth-century bearers commonly use ''de'' forms that can denote association with the place;
* repeated use for named people, including clerics, merchants, burgesses and royal officers, gives the designation personal identifying force;
* by the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, unprefixed forms such as ''Glasgw'' occur and proved family relationships show hereditary surname use.

This transition need not represent one continuous male line. Separate people could independently acquire the same locative from origin, residence, office or institutional association.

== Origin hypotheses ==

John's possible kinship with Gamelin and proposed connections to Walter Comyn or Walter Capellanus remain origin hypotheses. No inspected record states those relationships or connects the Glasgow bearers genealogically to those men. ''Capellanus'' is a Latin occupational title meaning chaplain, not evidence of a family name or lineage.

Norman, Comyn, Duffield, FitzAlan and specific Y-DNA origin theories remain unproved without a document-by-document pedigree to a tested modern line.
